title: A Study on the Impact of Temperature-Dependent Ferroelectric Switching Behavior in 3D Memory Architecture
problem: Hafnium Zirconium Oxide (HZO) FeRAM in 3D neural network accelerators suffers from thermal stress as on-chip temperatures rise during operation. Temperature-dependent ferroelectric switching behavior has not been well characterized in 3D memory architectures.
motivation: High-density 3D memory in AI accelerators raises on-chip temperature significantly. Understanding and exploiting temperature-dependent ferroelectric properties could enable dynamic write voltage optimization for reduced energy consumption.
method: Experimental device characterization and circuit/architecture-level simulation of HZO-based FeRAM in 3D memory architectures. Study of temperature-dependent polarization switching behavior through thermal impact analysis. Dynamic write voltage optimization exploiting temperature-activated switching mechanisms.
key_novelty: First study exploiting temperature-dependent ferroelectric switching to reduce FeRAM write energy in 3D memory architectures for neural network accelerators.
contributions: Characterized temperature-dependent polarization switching in HZO FeRAM
Demonstrated dynamic write voltage reduction with temperature increase
27.6% reduction in access energy per bit when on-chip temperature rises from 300K to 351K
Dynamic write voltage strategy enabling energy-efficient 3D FeRAM operation
Architecture-level simulation framework for thermal-aware memory design
limitations: Single device platform (HZO); generalizability to other ferroelectric materials (PZT, BFO) unclear
Temperature range limited to 300-351K; behavior at extreme corners not explored
No detailed breakdown of energy components (switching, leakage, access time)
Dynamic voltage switching overhead and latency not quantified
Reliability impact of repeated thermal cycling not addressed
Scalability to larger 3D arrays or full SoC-level thermal variations not demonstrated
No comparison with other thermal management approaches (active cooling, thermal-aware placement)
